title: Given a string and a dictionary of words, determine whether the string can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.
shortTitle: Word Break — can a string be segmented into dictionary words

s1_definition.profdef: 1D DP where dp[i] means "the prefix of length i can be segmented." dp[0]=true, and dp[i] is true if some j<i has dp[j]=true and the substring from j to i is in the dictionary. Time O(n² · L) with substring/lookup cost, space O(n).
s1_definition.analogy: A payments parser at National Bank of India receives a concatenated instruction string with no separators and must check whether it splits cleanly into known command words. A position is reachable if an earlier reachable position is followed by a valid word ending here.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i] true if some dp[j] true and substring(j,i) is a dictionary word.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 1D DP where dp[i] means "the prefix of length i can be segmented." dp[0]=true, and dp[i] is true if some j<i has dp[j]=true and the substring from j to i is in the dictionary. Time O(n² · L) with substring/lookup cost, space O(n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A payments parser at National Bank of India receives a concatenated instruction string with no separators and must check whether it splits cleanly into known command words. A position is reachable if an earlier reachable position is followed by a valid word ending here.

**One line to remember:** dp[i] true if some dp[j] true and substring(j,i) is a dictionary word.

sections.s2_technical:
Put the dictionary into a HashSet for constant-time lookups. Create a boolean dp of size n+1 with dp[0]=true, meaning the empty prefix is trivially segmentable. For each end position i from 1 to n, try every start j from 0 to i−1: if dp[j] is true and the substring from j to i is a dictionary word, mark dp[i] true and stop the inner loop. For example: `if (dp[j] && dict.contains(s.substring(j, i))) { dp[i] = true; break; }`.

The reasoning is that a prefix is segmentable exactly when it ends with a valid word whose starting point is itself a segmentable prefix. The answer is dp[n].

The time is O(n²) substring attempts, each costing up to O(L) for the substring and lookup, and space is O(n). A senior nuance is that the related "Word Break II" that returns all sentences can blow up exponentially, so it needs memoized backtracking rather than simple DP.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a legacy channel sends payment instructions as one concatenated string of command words with no separators, and the parser must verify it cleanly splits into known commands before executing. This is exactly how Word Break works.

Problem 2 — A greedy left-to-right longest-word match can fail because an early wrong cut blocks a valid later split. This is exactly why DP that remembers every reachable boundary is needed.

The mini-project builds an `InstructionParser`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input string is paycreditfee with dictionary pay, credit, fee.

Step 1: dp of zero is true representing the empty prefix.

Step 2: At position three the substring pay is a word and dp of zero is true, so dp of three becomes true.

Step 3: At position nine the substring credit from position three is a word and dp of three is true, so dp of nine becomes true.

Step 4: At position twelve the substring fee from position nine is a word and dp of nine is true, so dp of twelve becomes true.

Step 5: The answer is dp of twelve which is true, while payxyz cannot reach the end so it returns false.

```text
2026-10-27T02:20:00Z [INFO] 'payxyz' → false
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Break is a one-dimensional dynamic programming problem over the positions of the string. I define dp of i as whether the prefix of length i can be segmented into dictionary words. I put the dictionary into a hash set for constant-time lookups, and I set dp of zero to true because the empty prefix is trivially segmentable.

For each end position I look back at every start position and ask two things: is that start itself a segmentable boundary, and is the substring between the start and the end a dictionary word. If both hold, the end position is segmentable. The intuition is that a prefix is segmentable exactly when it ends in a valid word whose starting point is also segmentable, and the answer is dp of the full length.

In my project at National Bank of India, a legacy channel sent payment instructions as one concatenated string of command words with no separators, and the parser had to verify a clean split before executing. A greedy longest-word match could fail because an early wrong cut blocks a valid later split, so I used this DP that remembers every reachable boundary, and I note that the variant returning all sentences needs memoized backtracking because the output can be exponential.
